summary: Defines a method for a protected resource to ask an OAuth 2.0 authorization server whether a token is currently active and to get information about it. This conveys the authorization context from the server to the resource.

plainLanguage.summary: A guard calls the office to ask whether a visitor's pass is still good and who it belongs to.

questions: how to check if an oauth token is active
what does the active field mean in token introspection
how to secure the introspection endpoint
subtitle: How a protected API asks the authorization server whether an OAuth 2.0 token is still good, and what it grants.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 tokens are opaque to clients, and OAuth 2.0 itself gives a resource server no standard way to learn whether a token is valid or what it allows.
tldr.mechanism: The protected resource sends the token in an HTTP POST to an introspection endpoint on the authorization server, which answers with a JSON document whose required member is active, plus optional metadata such as scope, client_id and exp.
tldr.outcome: Resource servers get live, centrally controlled token state without needing to parse tokens, at the cost of one extra call (which they may cache) and a need to protect the endpoint.

sections.title: The Gap in OAuth 2.0
sections.content:
In OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) the contents of a token are opaque to the client. Yet a protected resource needs metadata about the token to decide whether to serve a request: is it still valid, which scopes were approved, who authorized it, and which client it was issued to.

OAuth 2.0 defines no way for a resource server to learn this from the authorization server. Deployments had filled the gap with structured tokens such as JWT (RFC 7519) or proprietary mechanisms like shared databases and protected enterprise service buses.

This RFC defines token introspection: a protocol for an authorized protected resource to query the authorization server about a token. It works whether or not the information is carried in the token itself, so it can be used with or without structured token values.
sections.plainLanguage: The token is a sealed envelope that nobody but the office can read. This RFC gives the guard a phone line to the office to ask what the envelope means.

sections.title: The Introspection Endpoint
sections.content:
The introspection endpoint is an OAuth 2.0 endpoint that takes a token and returns a JSON document describing it, including whether it is currently active. What counts as active depends on the authorization server, but it is commonly a token that the server issued, that has not expired, that has not been revoked, and that is valid for use at the protected resource making the call.

The endpoint MUST be protected by a transport-layer security mechanism. How the protected resource finds the endpoint is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoint is the office's front desk. You hand over a pass and the desk tells you whether it still works.

sections.title: The Introspection Request
sections.content:
The protected resource calls the endpoint with an HTTP POST whose parameters are sent as application/x-www-form-urlencoded data. There are two defined parameters:

  • token (REQUIRED): the string value of the token. For access tokens this is the access_token value from the token endpoint; for refresh tokens it is the refresh_token value. Other token types are out of scope.
  • token_type_hint (OPTIONAL): a hint about the token type that can speed up lookup. If the server cannot find the token using the hint, it MUST search across all the token types it supports. The server MAY ignore the hint.

The endpoint MAY accept other optional parameters to give context, for example the IP address of the client using the protected resource. Their definition is left to service documentation or extensions. If the server cannot decide the state of a token without such extra information, it SHOULD answer that the token is not active.

To prevent token scanning attacks, the endpoint MUST require some form of authorization, such as client authentication as in RFC 6749 or a separate OAuth 2.0 bearer token (RFC 6750).
sections.plainLanguage: You give the desk the pass number, and maybe a note saying what kind of pass it is. The desk also wants to see your own badge first, so strangers cannot keep guessing pass numbers.

sections.title: The Introspection Response
sections.content:
The server answers with a JSON object in application/json format. Only active is required; it is a boolean saying whether the token is currently active. A true value generally means the server issued the token, the resource owner has not revoked it, and it is within its time window of validity.

The optional members are scope (a space-separated list of scopes), client_id, username (a human-readable identifier for the resource owner), token_type, the integer timestamps exp, iat and nbf (seconds since January 1 1970 UTC), and the JWT-defined sub, aud, iss and jti. Implementations MAY add their own top-level members; names meant to be used across domains MUST be registered in the new "OAuth Token Introspection Response" registry.

The server MAY answer different protected resources differently for the same request. For instance, it may limit which scopes it reveals so that a resource learns no more about the wider network than it needs.

If the call is properly authorized but the token is not active, does not exist, or this resource may not introspect it, the server MUST return active set to false. It SHOULD NOT add anything else, including why the token is inactive.
sections.plainLanguage: The desk replies with a card. The only line that is always there says yes or no. If the answer is yes, the card may also say who the pass belongs to and what rooms it opens. If the answer is no, the desk says nothing more.

sections.title: Errors Versus Inactive Tokens
sections.content:
An inactive token is not an error. A properly formed and authorized query about an inactive or invalid token, or one the resource is not allowed to know about, gets a normal response with active set to false.

Errors are about the caller. If the protected resource authenticates with client credentials and they are invalid, the server responds with HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) as in RFC 6749. If it uses a bearer token that lacks sufficient privileges or is otherwise invalid, the server also responds with HTTP 401, as described in RFC 6750.
sections.plainLanguage: If the pass is bad, that is a normal answer: "no". It is only an error if the guard's own badge does not work.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Because the resource server relies on the authorization server to judge a token, the server MUST perform all applicable checks: expiry, whether the valid period has started, revocation, signature validation for signed tokens, and whether the token may be used at the calling resource server. A missed check could lead the resource server to a wrong security decision.

The endpoint MUST require authentication of the protected resources that call it and SHOULD require them to be specifically authorized. The server MUST support TLS 1.2 and the client MUST check the server certificate. An authorization server MAY refuse HTTP GET so that token values do not leak into server logs through query parameters.

Caching is a trade-off. A short cache gives fresher data at the cost of more traffic; a long cache reduces load but a revoked token could still be accepted in the meantime. Highly sensitive environments can disable caching. If the response contains exp, it MUST NOT be cached beyond that time.

On privacy, responses may contain user identifiers, so measures MUST be taken to prevent disclosure to unintended parties. One method is to return opaque, service-specific identifiers, possibly different for each protected resource. Omitting sensitive information is the simplest approach.
sections.plainLanguage: The office has to check everything before saying yes. If the guard remembers an old answer for too long, a pass that was cancelled might still get someone in. Also, the office should not hand out more personal details than the guard needs.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
The RFC establishes the "OAuth Token Introspection Response" registry. New names are registered by Specification Required after a two-week review period on a mailing list, on the advice of one or more Designated Experts, who may approve a registration earlier once they are satisfied a specification will be published.

The initial contents are the twelve members defined in the response section: active, username, client_id, scope, token_type, exp, iat, nbf, sub, aud, iss and jti, each with the IESG as change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a public list of the names allowed on the reply card, so everyone uses the same words for the same things.
